(1) Live overlay, used by default: page 1 is rasterised once at no more than 1 px per PDF point, capped at 4096 px / 32 MB (iOS PDFRasteriser, PDFOverlay.swift:69-141; Android PdfPageRenderer.renderFirstPage, PdfPageRenderer.kt:44-98). The raster is pinned to the map by projecting page corners through the PDF-to-lon/lat affine and then Web Mercator. iOS uses a 3-corner CGAffineTransform on a UIImageView (PDFOverlay.swift:253-275) under a dark mask. Android uses a 4-corner setPolyToPoly (CustomMapOverlays.kt:858-882). No basemap is drawn under a PDF on either platform. (2) Optional bake: every tile's lon/lat box is mapped back through the inverse affine, split into strips no taller than 0.25 deg of latitude (the U13 fix), rendered to 256 px opaque PNGs and written to MBTiles (iOS PDFTiler.swift, Android PdfTiler.kt). TileMapView then shows them at round(zoom), clamped to the file's min/max, with overzoom by scaling. Pinch zoom is hard-clamped to the source's min/max.

Solid on both: the Web Mercator and tile math (lonToTileX, tileYToLat, tileRange, TMS flip) match between platforms. Tile layout, heading rotation and the 0.5-unit overlap that hides seams are correct. Strip latitude correction is right for north-up calibrations. Rasters are memory-bounded, the .partial publish is atomic with cleanup, the off-page tile check works, and Android's load coordinator scopes each load to its source generation. Tile zoom rounding is the same on both.

Where it breaks: the tiler drops rotation, the live overlay is linear in Mercator and limited to 72 dpi, Android's bake zoom is 3 levels lower than iOS's, and the page-box and rotation assumptions differ between platforms (details below).

Outside D3, noticed while checking the sample (please route to D1/D2):
- (a) The USGS_SF_North.pdf "Map Layers" viewport has LPTS values from -0.00708 to 1.00708, and both parsers reject any LPTS outside [0,1] (GeoPDFReader.swift:349-350, GeoPdfParser.kt:206). The sheet is marked rejected on iOS and falls back to camera-centre bounds on both platforms; listed as D3-17.
- (b) Android pdfPointFor (MapScreenHelpers.kt:65-80) turns calibration taps into PDF coordinates using a linear coverage-bbox ratio, not the inverse of the affine placement actually drawn. Re-calibrating a GeoPDF or an already-calibrated or rotated sheet therefore records wrong PDF points.

Numbers for the USGS 1:24k sheet at 37.8 N: 72-dpi source pixel = 8.46 m. At z16 (1.887 m/pt) one source pixel covers 13.5 device pixels on a 3x screen. Android bakes z11-13 (15.1 m per tile pixel) and iOS bakes z10-16 (1.89 m per tile pixel).

findings.title: Tiler maps each strip through an axis-aligned bounding rect, dropping rotation and shear, so rotated calibrations bake misregistered tiles with jogs at every seam
findings.description: For each strip, both tilers push the 4 lon/lat band corners through the inverse affine, take the min/max bounding rect in PDF space, and map that rect onto the tile band with only scale and translate. iOS uses ctx.scaleBy/translateBy; Android uses Matrix.setRectToRect(FILL). When the affine has off-diagonal terms (rotation or shear), the band's true footprint in PDF space is a parallelogram inside that rect. The tile corners land on the rect's corners, not the parallelogram's, and each tile is squeezed by 1/(cos t + sin t). The error is a fixed fraction of the tile, so it appears at every zoom level and flips sign across seams. The live overlays (iOS CGAffineTransform, Android polyToPoly) keep rotation, so the baked map disagrees with the preview. Simulated (scratchpad audit/tilerot.py): 0.35 deg rotation gives 1.56 px max misplacement and a 2.2 px seam jog; 1.68 deg (an MGA grid-aligned 1:25k sheet at a zone edge) gives 7.5 px / 10.6 px (15 m / 21 m at z16); a 4 deg crooked scan gives 17.9 px / 25.3 px (27 m / 38 m at z16, 107 m / 152 m at z14). The USGS sample fits almost exactly north-up (0.001 deg), which is why it hides this.
findings.failure_scenario: The user photographs or scans a paper 1:25k map about 4 deg crooked, calibrates it with 4 fiduciaries (mode b), and bakes offline tiles. Every tile is shifted by up to about 18 px. Roads and printed grid lines break by about 25 px at every tile boundary, and the MGRS overlay is 25-40 m off the printed grid at z16. The live preview before baking looked correct.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the full per-strip affine (tile pixel to PDF point) from three band corners mapped through the inverse affine, not from the bounding rect. On iOS, ctx.concatenate(CGAffineTransform(a,b,c,d,tx,ty)) with the inverse of that mapping. On Android, Matrix.setPolyToPoly(src=3 band-corner PDF points in page space, dst=3 tile-band pixel corners, count=3). Keep the bounding rect only for the off-page check.
findings.proving_test: Pure host test on both platforms. Extract the strip mapping into a function that returns the PDF point drawn at tile pixel (u,v). Fixture: an affine with 4 deg clockwise rotation at 51N, 8.8 m/pt. For tile z16 containing the sheet centre, assert |mapped(corner) - inverse.apply(tileCornerLonLat)| < 0.5 tile px (currently 17.9 px). Instrumented variant: synthetic PDF with a 1-pt line along a known meridian, calibrate with rotated fiduciaries, bake, then check the line's pixel column at the shared edge of two horizontally adjacent tiles differs by 1 px or less (currently about 25 px).

findings.title: Android bake maxZoom comes from 72-dpi page points and is floored, and the camera is clamped to it, so a baked 1:24k sheet stops at z13 and is coarser than the live preview
findings.description: zoomRange sets maxZoom = floor(log2(pageWidthPoints/lonSpan*360/256)). pageWidth is PdfRenderer points (72 dpi), so the tile level is chosen to be no finer than a 72-dpi raster, and floor() makes it coarser. The minzoom and maxzoom written to the MBTiles then become OfflineRasterTileSource.min/max. CustomMapScreen passes those into MapItemTouchOverlayCustom, which coerces pinch zoom to [minZoom, maxZoom]. For USGS SF North (1728 pt page, 0.1662 deg lon) Android bakes z11-13, 38 tiles in total, at 15.1 m per tile pixel. The live overlay it replaces is 8.46 m per pixel, and iOS bakes the same sheet at z10-16 (1.89 m per pixel). Other sheet scales (audit/zr.py): 1:50k Android z13 (15.8 m) vs iOS z15 (4.0 m); 1:250k Android z11 (48.6 m) vs iOS z13 (12.2 m). Baked tiles are also 256 px at 1 px per dp, so on a 2.6-3x screen each tile pixel is magnified again.
findings.failure_scenario: An Android user bakes the USGS 1:24k sheet for offline use. After activation, pinch-in stops at z13, where a 411 dp phone screen still spans about 6.2 km. 7-pt map labels are about 4 tile pixels tall and unreadable, and 1000 m grid ticks and contours are mush. The same PDF on iOS bakes to z16 and is readable.
findings.suggested_fix: Choose maxZoom from the map's paper scale or content resolution, not 72-dpi points. For example, target tile ground resolution at or below scale*0.1 mm (about 300 dpi of paper), bounded by the tile budget, or reuse the iOS budget rule so both platforms produce the same pyramid. Put the rule in a shared fixture in testdata. Separately, allow camera overzoom 2-3 levels past an offline source's maxZoom (TileMath already scales tiles). Consider baking 512 px tiles, or picking tileZoom = round(zoom + log2(density)), for crisp display at 2-3x.
findings.proving_test: JVM test (make PdfTiler.zoomRange internal): PdfPageInfo(1728,2088) with coverage lat 37.72885-37.88818, lon -122.52012 to -122.35390 should give maxZoom >= 16 (currently 13). Add a cross-platform fixture asserting iOS and Android return the same (minZoom, maxZoom). Also: applyCustomMapTransform(camera zoom 13, zoomChange=2f, minZoom=11.0, maxZoom=13.0).zoom is 13.0, showing zoom-in is blocked.

findings.title: Live PDF overlay is placed linearly in Web Mercator, so the mid-sheet error grows with the square of sheet height (4.8 m at 1:24k, about 295 m at 1:250k)
findings.description: Both overlays project only the page corners (affine then Mercator) and stretch the raster linearly between them: iOS with a CGAffineTransform from TL/TR/BL plus the centroid, Android with a 4-point setPolyToPoly. PDF to lon/lat is affine, but lat to Mercator y is not linear, so interior points drift north or south. For a north-up sheet the 4 projected corners form a rectangle, so Android's homography reduces to the same affine and both platforms err equally. The tiler corrects this with 0.25 deg strips (U13); the default overlay path does not. Worst misplacement, near mid-sheet (audit/overlay.py, overlay2.py): USGS 1:24k SF 4.8 m; 1:50k 15' sheet at -34 lat 10.3 m; 1:100k 30' sheet at 50N 73 m; 1:250k 1 deg x 1.5 deg at 50N 295 m (173 m at -35). This is on top of any fit residual, and it moves the printed grid relative to the MGRS overlay.
findings.failure_scenario: A user imports a georeferenced 1:250k JOG-style sheet (1 deg of latitude) and turns on the MGRS grid. The corners line up, but across the middle band the printed 10 km grid sits about 300 m south of TacMap's grid, and any waypoint dropped on a printed feature is recorded about 300 m off. On a 1:50k sheet the offset is about 10 m, which is visible as about 5 pt at z16.
findings.suggested_fix: Draw the overlay with the same latitude-strip decomposition as the tiler. On Android, use Canvas.drawBitmapMesh with a grid of vertices at camera.screenPoint(affine.apply(pdfPoint)); 8x16 is plenty. On iOS, split the image into N horizontal sublayers (contentsRect bands), each placed with its own 3-point affine from its band corners, or draw strips in draw(_:). Enforce that the error is under 1 px at the max zoom.
findings.proving_test: iOS XCTest: MapCamera at z16 centred on 50.5N/-2.25; PDF render rect 1000x1000 with an axis-aligned lon/lat affine covering 50-51N, 3-1.5W. Build PDFImageOverlayView and call updateFrame. Compare view.convert(localPoint(forPDFPoint: mid), to: host) with camera.screenPoint(for: affine.apply(mid)). Assert < 1 pt; currently about 194 pt (295 m at 1.52 m/pt). Android: extract the corner/matrix builder from PdfGroundLayer into a pure function and assert the same bound.

findings.title: Live overlay is rasterised at no more than 72 dpi, so text and grid lines blur at field zooms and fiduciary taps are imprecise
findings.description: boundedPDFRasterSize and boundedPdfRenderSize both take scale = min(1, dimensionCap, memoryCap). The page is never rendered above 1 px per PDF point, even when the 4096 px / 32 MB budget allows 1.52x for USGS. The live overlay is the default display (baking is optional) and is also the surface for fiduciary calibration. For the USGS 1:24k sheet one raster pixel is 8.46 m on the ground, so on a 3x device: z13 = 1.7 device px per source pixel (already upscaled when the whole sheet fits), z15 = 6.7, z16 = 13.5, z18 = 54. Printed 0.1 mm grid lines (2.4 m) become faint anti-aliased smears at 72 dpi. A letter or A4 PDF wrapping a 300-dpi scan is shown at a quarter of its linear resolution. Nothing re-renders the visible region at screen resolution; PdfPageRenderer.renderFirstPageRegion exists but has no caller.
findings.failure_scenario: The user imports a 1:25k scan (A4 page, 300-dpi image) to calibrate and zooms to z17 to tap a grid intersection. The intersection is a 1-2 source-pixel blur spanning about 20-50 device px, so the tap can be several metres off. Labels and spot heights are unreadable at any zoom where the map is useful. This is the same on both platforms.
findings.suggested_fix: Render the visible region on demand at screen resolution: on iOS a CATiledLayer or region re-render on camera idle via PDFKit; on Android renderFirstPageRegion for the viewport on camera idle. Keep the current 72-dpi raster only as an instant fallback. At minimum remove the min(1, ...) cap so the whole budget is used, and pick the scale from the embedded image DPI for scanned PDFs.
findings.proving_test: iOS: PDFMapSource(url: USGS).renderedImage() is 1727x2031 px for a 1727.96x2031.31 pt crop (1 px/pt). Assert that the overlay's source-pixel density at camera z16 on a 3x screen is at least 0.5 source px per device px (currently 0.074). Android: boundedPdfRenderSize(1728, 2088) returns 1728x2088 (scale 1.0) though the memory cap allows 1.52; assert the scale is above 1 when the budget allows.

findings.title: Android treats PdfRenderer page space (CropBox-relative, int-truncated size) as raw PDF user space, so GeoPDFs with a cropped or offset page box are misregistered in the overlay and baked tiles
findings.description: GeoPdfParser returns correspondences in raw user space via PDFBox (BBox, LPTS, Neatline). PdfRenderer (pdfium FPDF_RenderPageBitmapWithMatrix + GetDisplayMatrix) renders in page space: origin at the CropBox top-left (MediaBox if there is no CropBox), y down, with getWidth()/getHeight() truncated to Int. PdfGroundLayer pins the bitmap to transform.apply(0..pw, 0..ph), and PdfTiler flips with h = pageHeight (Int), both assuming the crop box starts at (0,0) with integer size. Result: any CropBox or MediaBox lower-left offset shifts the whole map by that offset. A fractional page height (A4 is 841.89 pt) shifts everything by the fractional part, 0.89 pt, about 7.8 m at 1:25k. iOS draws .mediaBox in raw user space and gets the CropBox case right, so the platforms diverge. Manual calibration is self-consistent on Android because the tap mapping uses the same assumed frame; the GeoPDF path is the one hit.
findings.failure_scenario: A GeoPDF whose collar was trimmed in Acrobat (MediaBox [0 0 1728 2088], CropBox [36 36 1692 2052]) is imported on Android. The sheet is drawn 36 pt west and 36 pt south of its true position, about 305 m each way at 1:24k (430 m total), and baked tiles have the same offset. The same file on iOS lines up. An untrimmed A4 1:25k GeoPDF is about 8 m south on Android.
findings.suggested_fix: At import, read cropBox (fall back to mediaBox) with PDFBox and store x0, y0 and the float width/height in PdfPageInfo. Convert user space to page space as (x - x0, (y0 + h) - y) in PdfTiler.pageRectForBand, and place PdfGroundLayer corners at T(x0, y0+h), T(x0+w, y0+h), T(x0+w, y0), T(x0, y0). Pass an explicit render transform built from the float size, not relying on the default stretch against int getWidth().
findings.proving_test: androidTest: generate a PDF with MediaBox [0 0 600 800], CropBox [50 50 550 750], an Adobe VP (BBox [100 100 500 700], GPTS at known lat/lon, LPTS 0/1) and a 2-pt black cross at user (100,100). Import it and locate the cross in the PdfGroundLayer bitmap. Map that pixel through the layer's corner transform and assert it is within 1 px of the projected GPTS corner (currently off by 50 pt of map scale). Repeat on the baked tile containing the corner. Second case: MediaBox [0 0 595.276 841.89] with no crop; expect less than 0.1 pt shift.

findings.title: iOS imports /Rotate pages and non-zero-origin MediaBoxes, but PDFKit's draw(with:to:) applies rotation and box origin itself, so the raster no longer matches the unrotated user space the affine and crop use (Android rejects rotated pages)
findings.description: Needs device confirmation; this rests on the documented PDFKit contract, not a device run. PDFPage.draw(with:to:) is documented to take page rotation into account and to draw relative to the box bounds. PDFRasteriser and PDFTiler compute their CTM from the unrotated bounds(for: .mediaBox) and subtract renderRect.minX/minY themselves, then call page.draw(with: .mediaBox). For /Rotate 90/270 the content is rotated inside a canvas sized for the unrotated page, so part is clipped and the GeoPDF affine (raw user space) no longer matches the pixels. For a MediaBox with non-zero origin the origin is subtracted twice, shifting content by the origin. iOS explicitly accepts rotated pages: PDFImportSmokeTests only asserts the raster is non-empty. Android refuses them in preflight with a user-facing message.
findings.failure_scenario: A scanner-produced landscape GeoPDF stored as a portrait MediaBox with /Rotate 90 imports on iOS. The overlay shows a rotated, half-clipped sheet in a portrait frame and GeoPDF registration is wrong; the same file is cleanly rejected on Android. Separately, a PDF with MediaBox [18 18 630 810] renders shifted 18 pt (about 150 m at 1:24k) on iOS.
findings.suggested_fix: Match Android: reject page.rotation != 0 in PDFMapImporter.copyAndValidate or the import worker. Or apply rotation consistently: use page.bounds(for:) rotated by page.rotation for canvas size and transform the affine's user space the same way. For the origin, translate by (mediaBox.minX - renderRect.minX, mediaBox.minY - renderRect.minY), not -renderRect.origin.
findings.proving_test: XCTest: raw PDF with MediaBox [0 0 600 400], /Rotate 90, a VP georef and a filled red 10x10 square at user (50,50). Import, render via PDFRasteriser, find the red centroid, convert with PDFImageOverlayView.pdfPoint mapping, and assert about (55,55) within 1 pt, or assert the import throws. Second test: MediaBox [100 100 700 500] with the square at user (150,150); assert the round trip is within 1 pt.

findings.title: Android offline-tile bake cannot be cancelled (modal dialog, no button) and re-opens the PDF and re-parses the page for every tile and strip
findings.description: The progress AlertDialog has onDismissRequest = { /* non-cancelable while baking */ } and an empty confirmButton, so no UI can cancel. PdfTiler's ensureActive() checks, commented as honouring the Cancel button, cannot be reached from the UI (iOS has a Cancel button). Per tile, renderFirstPageStrips opens a new ParcelFileDescriptor and a new PdfRenderer (document load), then calls openPage(0) once per strip. pdfium's FPDF_LoadPage parses the full content stream, so a heavy 40 MB USGS page is parsed once per tile, and up to 16 times per low-zoom tile. The KDoc claim that this is cheap next to the one-time parse is wrong because the parse happens every time. Today the tile count is tiny (38 for USGS, see D3-02); once maxZoom is fixed the bake runs about 2,500 page parses behind an uncancellable modal. The job also runs on the composable's rememberCoroutineScope, not a foreground service or WorkManager.
findings.failure_scenario: The user starts a bake of a large scanned PDF and realises it will take many minutes. Back and taps outside do nothing and there is no Cancel, so the only exit is force-killing the app, which leaves a stale .partial file. After D3-02 is fixed the USGS sheet needs about 2,300 tiles times one full page parse each, with no way out.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Cancel button that cancels the Job; PdfTiler already cleans up on cancellation. Open one ParcelFileDescriptor, PdfRenderer and Page for the whole bake and reuse it for all tiles and strips, rendering serially (PdfRenderer allows one open page). Run the bake in a WorkManager foreground worker with a notification so it survives backgrounding.
findings.proving_test: androidTest (Compose): trigger onGenerateTiles, then assert a node with text 'Cancel' exists and clicking it clears tilingProgress and deletes the .partial file (fails today). Unit or instrumented: wrap openDescriptor with a counter, bake a 3x3-tile fixture, and assert PdfRenderer is constructed once (currently equal to tile count, and openPage is called once per strip).

findings.title: Pinch zoom is hard-clamped to the offline source's zoom range while programmatic targets are not, so the first pinch snaps the map several levels
findings.description: Gesture zoom is coerced to [source.minZoom, source.maxZoom] (Android applyCustomMapTransform; iOS handlePinch). Programmatic moves ignore that range: Android frameCameraFor and centreOnUser fly to z15 or z13, and iOS flyTo clamps only to 2...19, with centreOnUser at 1500 m being about z16.1. After activating a baked Android sheet (max 13) with the user inside it, the camera is placed at z15, which shows 4x-overzoomed blurry tiles. The first pinch, or any two-finger pan with a tiny scale change, jumps it to z13. Zooming out is equally blocked below minZoom (z11 Android, z10 iOS for USGS). TileMath already supports overzoom and underzoom by scaling, so the clamp is not needed for offline sources.
findings.failure_scenario: On Android, the user bakes and activates the sheet, which lands at z15. They start a gentle pinch to zoom in and the map jumps out two levels to z13. On iOS, 'centre on me' goes to z16.1 over a z16 bake and the next pinch snaps back.
findings.suggested_fix: For offline (baked) sources, allow camera zoom from about 2 up to maxZoom + 3 (or 22) and rely on TileMath's clamped tileZoom for overzoom and underzoom. Otherwise clamp programmatic targets to the same range so gestures never snap.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM: applyCustomMapTransform(camera zoom=15.0, zoomChange=1.02f, minZoom=11.0, maxZoom=13.0).zoom should be about 15.03 (currently 13.0). iOS: TileMapView with a fake RasterTileSource(maxZoom 16), camera.zoom = 18, a synthetic pinch of scale 1.01; assert zoom about 18.01 (currently 16).

findings.title: iOS live overlay's floored raster size plus uniform min scale leaves up to 1 px of unmapped slack, shifting the sheet up to about 7 m (USGS) and offsetting manual-calibration bakes
findings.description: boundedPDFRasterSize floors each dimension. PDFRasteriser then uses one uniform scale = min(iw/W, ih/H) and anchors content at the bottom-left, so the other axis leaves up to 1 px unfilled at the top or right. PDFImageOverlayView (placement, pdfPoint, localPoint) assumes the image fills pdfRenderRect exactly. For the USGS Map Layers crop (1727.96 x 2031.31 pt) the image is 1727x2031, s = 0.999444, and the crop's top edge lands on row 0.82. Content is drawn up to 0.82 pt south of its true place: about 7 m at the top of the 1:24k sheet, 14 m for a 1:50k A0 sheet (audit/floorerr.py). Manual calibration taps use the same assumed mapping, so the fit absorbs the offset. PDFTiler renders with exact geometry, so the baked tiles then sit up to 0.82 pt from the calibrated points.
findings.failure_scenario: On iOS the imported USGS sheet's printed grid along the top of the map sits about 7 m south of the MGRS overlay; this adds to D3-03. After a manual calibration and bake, the baked tiles are offset from the fiduciaries by up to the same amount.
findings.suggested_fix: Use independent scales sx = iw/W and sy = ih/H in PDFRasteriser. Or keep uniform scaling and give PDFImageOverlayView the rect actually covered by content (renderRect scaled by s), not assume full fill.
findings.proving_test: XCTest: page 1728x2088 with a 1-pt black horizontal line at user y = 2087.0; PDFRasteriser.render(cropRect: (0, 56.69373, 1727.95998, 2031.30627)). Find the line's centre row r. Assert |r - localPoint(forPDFPoint:(x, 2087)).y * (ih/bounds.height)| <= 0.25 px (currently about 0.82 px).

findings.title: iOS bake progress and cancel live in LayersSheet @State: dismissing the sheet orphans the bake, allows duplicate bakes, and a lock during background tracking can fail the bake
findings.description: tilingTask and tilingProgress are @State of the sheet, and the detached Task is not tied to the view's lifetime. When the user swipes the sheet down mid-bake, the Cancel button and progress disappear. Reopening shows 'Generate Offline Tiles…' again, which can start a second concurrent bake writing another .partial. The orphaned task later switches the map source unannounced. There is no UIApplication background task, and the offline_tiles directory is created with FileProtectionType.complete, which the .partial SQLite file will normally inherit. With background location enabled (UIBackgroundModes location) the app keeps running when the phone auto-locks during a long bake, and SQLite writes to a .complete file fail about 10 s after lock. writer.hadError then discards the whole bake. The lock-failure chain needs device confirmation.
findings.failure_scenario: The user starts a 2,300-tile USGS bake, swipes the sheet away to keep working, and reopens it: no progress, and a new Generate button that starts a second bake. Or the phone auto-locks during the bake while tracking is on, and minutes later it fails with 'Couldn't generate offline tiles'.
findings.suggested_fix: Move bake state (task, progress, cancel) into MapViewModel or an app-level service and show it on the map chrome. Disable Generate while a bake is running. Create the .partial with .completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication (the final file already gets that). Wrap the bake in beginBackgroundTask and consider isIdleTimerDisabled while it runs.
findings.proving_test: UI test: start a bake, swipe LayersSheet down, reopen, and assert the progress and Cancel UI are present (fails). Tap Generate again and assert Application Support/offline_tiles holds only one *.partial file (currently two). On a device with background tracking on, start a bake, lock the phone for 60 s, unlock, and expect success (confirm the failure first).

findings.title: No parent or child tile fallback: crossing a zoom level or panning shows dark holes until tiles load, and iOS decodes PNGs on the main thread in draw()
findings.description: Both renderers compute visible tiles only at the current rounded tileZoom and draw only cached tiles. A missing tile leaves the near-black background (0.07 white on iOS, 0xFF121212 on Android), even though the previous level's tiles are usually still in the cache (NSCache 400 entries, Android LRU 48 MB). tileZoom flips at every x.5, so pinching through a boundary blanks the whole viewport for a frame or more on each crossing, which is harsh against a mostly white topo sheet. On iOS, UIImage(data:) decodes lazily, so PNG decoding happens inside draw(_:) on the main thread for every newly arrived tile.
findings.failure_scenario: The user pinches slowly from z13.4 to z13.6 over a baked topo sheet. The whole map flashes dark and tiles pop back in; pinching back and forth around the boundary strobes. On iOS the arrival of 20 fresh tiles costs extra main-thread decode time in that frame.
findings.suggested_fix: When a tile is missing, draw the nearest cached ancestor (z-1..z-3) scaled to the tile's subrect, or cached descendants, before the background; keep the previous level until the new one is complete. On iOS, decode off-main with UIImage.preparingForDisplay() or an ImageIO forced decode in OfflineRasterTileSource.
findings.proving_test: iOS XCTest: TileMapView with a fake source that caches z13 tiles instantly and delays z14 by 300 ms. Set camera.zoom 13.4, draw, then 13.6 and immediately layer.render(in:). Assert fewer than 5% of pixels in the sheet area equal the background colour (currently about 100%). Android: equivalent Compose screenshot test with a delaying TileSource.

findings.title: Baked tiles are opaque white off-page with ragged borders that jump each zoom level; iOS bakes ignore the neatline crop the live overlay uses, and Android shows the whole collar
findings.description: Tiles are rendered opaque (iOS fmt.opaque = true plus a white fill; Android eraseColor(WHITE)) and saved as PNG. Tiles that partly overlap the page are white past the page edge, and tiles fully off the page are absent (dark background). The sheet is therefore framed by a white band up to one tile wide (256 pt), and its width changes at every zoom level. iOS bakes the full MediaBox over a 1.2x coverage box, while its live overlay is cropped to pdfCropRect (VP BBox / LGIDict neatline). The bake therefore contains legend and collar fragments cut at arbitrary tile edges that the preview never showed. Android's live overlay and bake both show the whole page, collar included, so the same GeoPDF looks different on the two platforms.
findings.failure_scenario: After baking an LGIDict GeoPDF on iOS, zooming from z12 to z15 shows a jagged white border and chopped legend pieces around the map that change shape at each level. On Android the same sheet is shown with its full white collar.
findings.suggested_fix: Render tiles with a transparent background (iOS fmt.opaque = false with a clear fill; Android eraseColor(TRANSPARENT)) and clip each tile to the neatline or crop polygon (pdfCropRect on iOS, the parsed neatline or VP BBox on Android). Apply the same crop in the Android live overlay for parity.
findings.proving_test: Bake a synthetic GeoPDF (neatline inset 72 pt from the page edge) on both platforms. Decode a tile straddling the neatline and assert pixels outside the neatline have alpha 0 (currently opaque white or collar content). Cross-platform: the fraction of non-transparent pixels in that tile is equal within 1%.

findings.title: iOS rasterises the PDF on the main thread inside updateUIView on first display and every cold launch, contrary to PDFMapSource's own contract
findings.description: syncPDF runs from updateUIView on the main thread and calls pdf.renderedImage() synchronously. renderedImage is documented as heavy and to be called off the main thread on first use, and cachedRenderedImage exists for exactly this but is never used. The import worker (ContentView.preparePDF) does not pre-render. On the first frame after import, and after every launch that restores a PDF, the main thread rasterises a 1728x2031 page of the 40 MB USGS PDF with PDFKit. If rendering returns nil, it is retried on every updateUIView. Android renders the same raster on Dispatchers.IO.
findings.failure_scenario: After importing USGS_SF_North.pdf, or relaunching with it active, the whole UI (map, buttons, sheets) freezes for the duration of the PDFKit rasterisation, likely a second or more on older iPhones, before the sheet appears.
findings.suggested_fix: In syncPDF, if cachedRenderedImage is nil, start a detached render and attach the overlay on completion (keyed by pdf.id), showing the dark mask or a spinner meanwhile. Optionally pre-render in the import worker.
findings.proving_test: XCTest: add a debug hook asserting !Thread.isMainThread inside the uncached branch of renderedImage(), then drive Coordinator.syncPDF with a PDFMapSource for the USGS sample; it fails today. Or use XCTClockMetric: time syncPDF on the main thread with an uncached USGS source and expect under 16 ms.

findings.title: iOS 'PDF overlay' visibility toggle does nothing in the custom renderer (regression from MKMapView removal)
findings.description: LayersSheet shows a Toggle bound to visibility.pdfOverlayVisible, which is persisted. TileMapContainer.updateUIView calls syncPDF(source:view:) without it, and syncPDF never reads it. The old MapContainerView path passed visible: visibility.pdfOverlayVisible (removed in 52dc3a7). Android has no such toggle.
findings.failure_scenario: A user switches the PDF off to see the drawings or grid alone, or to compare with symbols; the sheet stays drawn. Because the setting persists, it also misreports state after a relaunch.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass visibility.pdfOverlayVisible into syncPDF and set pdfView.isHidden and pdfMask.isHidden, or remove the toggle.
findings.proving_test: UI test: import a PDF, open Layers, switch the PDF toggle off, dismiss; assert the PDFImageOverlayView is hidden or removed (currently visible). Or a unit test driving Coordinator.syncPDF with a visible:false parameter once added.

findings.title: Live overlay has no mipmapping, so dense linework aliases and shimmers when zoomed out or while pinching
findings.description: The 1728x2088 raster is minified with plain bilinear filtering: iOS UIImageView's default CALayer minificationFilter is .linear, and Android uses Paint(FILTER_BITMAP_FLAG) on a bitmap without hasMipMap. At z11 over the USGS sheet the image is about 2.4x minified on a 3x screen, and more on tablets and at z10. Contours, roads and grid lines alias into moiré that crawls during pan and pinch.
findings.failure_scenario: Zooming out to see the whole sheet makes contour-dense areas shimmer and sparkle as the map moves.
findings.suggested_fix: iOS: layer.minificationFilter = .trilinear on PDFImageOverlayView. Android: bitmap.setHasMipMap(true) before the first draw.
findings.proving_test: iOS: assert pdfView.layer.minificationFilter == .trilinear. Android: assert the PdfGroundLayer bitmap hasMipMap(). Visual: render the overlay at z10.5 and compare against a box-filtered downsample reference (PSNR above 30 dB).

findings.title: No double-tap or one-finger zoom on either platform
findings.description: Zoom is pinch-only. Neither renderer installs a double-tap-to-zoom-in, two-finger-tap-to-zoom-out, or double-tap-and-drag gesture (no numberOfTapsRequired or onDoubleTap anywhere). The platforms behave the same, but one-handed or gloved field use cannot zoom.
findings.failure_scenario: A user holding the phone in one hand, or wearing gloves, cannot zoom into the PDF to read a grid reference.
findings.suggested_fix: iOS: a double-tap recognizer (zoom +1 about the tap point) with the single-tap editing recognizer required to fail, plus a two-finger tap for zoom -1. Android: detectTapGestures(onDoubleTap = …) in the interaction overlay.
findings.proving_test: UI test on each platform: double-tap the map centre and assert the published camera zoom increased by about 1 (currently unchanged).

findings.title: (Cross-dimension, for D1) Both GeoPDF parsers reject the bundled USGS sheet because its LPTS lie slightly outside [0,1], so the flagship sample falls back to camera-centre placement
findings.description: In samples/USGS_SF_North.pdf the 'Map Layers' viewport (BBox [0 2088 1727.96 56.69], Measure 424 0 R) has LPTS [-0.00708 1 0 -0.00514 1.00708 0 1 1.00514]; I inflated the ObjStm to confirm (audit/inspect3.py). Both parsers treat any LPTS outside [0,1] as malformed. The largest declared-GEO viewport becomes 'malformed' with area about 3.5e6, which is bigger than the two valid insets (about 5,000 and 3,300). The selection returns Rejected, and bounds(from:) / parse() return nil. iOS then uses fallbackBounds(centeredOn: camera) and Android an uncalibrated fallback box. There is no LGIDict to fall back on. The tests enshrine the rejection (LPTS 1.1 must fail). Reported here because every D3 render path depends on it; it belongs to D1.
findings.failure_scenario: Importing the documented sample on either platform gives a sheet placed at the camera centre with no georeferencing. The printed UTM grid cannot line up with the MGRS overlay until the user calibrates by hand.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept finite LPTS outside [0,1] (ISO 32000 lets control points extend past the viewport), for example within [-0.5, 1.5], or rank viewports by BBox area without using the LPTS range as a validity check. Add the USGS VP as a shared fixture.
findings.proving_test: iOS: XCTAssertNotNil(GeoPDFReader.bounds(from: samples/USGS_SF_North.pdf)) with SW about (37.7324, -122.5212) within 1e-3. Android: GeoPdfParser.parse(context, uri) is non-null with 4 correspondences. Both currently return nil or null.

verdicts.reasoning: Root cause: iOS stripRect (PDFTiler.swift:155-170) and Android pageRectForBand (PdfTiler.kt:187-219) both take the axis-aligned min/max box of the 4 inverse-mapped band corners. They then map that box onto the tile band using only scale and translate: iOS ctx.translateBy/scaleBy at PDFTiler.swift:207-209, Android Matrix.setRectToRect(FILL) at PdfPageRenderer.kt:183-184. Any b or d term in the full 6-term affine (AffineTransform2D.swift:14-23, fit at :111-113) is therefore lost. Nothing upstream stops rotated fits. By contrast, the live overlays keep the full basis: iOS PDFOverlay.swift:38-45, Android polyToPoly at CustomMapOverlays.kt:880. My own simulation (verify/rot.py; 51N, 8.8 m/pt, z16) matches the auditor's tile-pixel figures exactly: 0.35 deg gives 1.56 px error and a 2.21 px seam jog; 1.68 deg gives 7.51/10.61 px; 4 deg gives 17.86/25.26 px. At this latitude the metre values are a little smaller than the auditor's (4 deg: 27 m / 38 m at z16, which matches). Rotation is normal, not an edge case. Hand scans are rarely within 0.3 deg. Grid-aligned GeoPDFs are rotated by grid convergence (for example NZTopo50 or OS sheets about 1-3 deg from the central meridian). Baking is a normal user action from the Layers sheet. I kept critical because every tile at every zoom is misregistered and shows jogs at the seams.

PdfTiler.kt:224-226: maxZoom = floor(log2(pageWidth/lonSpan*360/256)). pageWidth is the integer page-point width from PdfRenderer (PdfPageRenderer.kt:68-75), so the tile level is tied to a 72-dpi raster and then floored. My script (verify/zr.py) gives Android (11,13) with 38 tiles and iOS (10,16) for the USGS coverage: 15.10 m per tile pixel at z13 vs 1.89 m at z16. The file's min/max zoom flows through OfflineTileMapSourceAndroid.kt:44-46 into OfflineRasterTileSource.min/maxZoom, then into MapItemTouchOverlayCustom (CustomMapScreen.kt:306-307). applyCustomMapTransform then coerces pinch zoom into that range (CustomMapTouch.kt:468). Pinch-in on a baked 1:24k sheet therefore stops at z13. Caveat: the USGS sample itself cannot be baked on either platform until D3-17 is fixed, because it has no transform. The numbers still apply to the same sheet after manual calibration and to any similar sheet.

iOS applyAffinePlacement (PDFOverlay.swift:253-275) projects 4 page corners through the affine and camera.screenPoint (Mercator), then fits one linear CGAffineTransform. Android PdfGroundLayer (CustomMapOverlays.kt:858-882) uses a 4-point setPolyToPoly. For a north-up sheet the projected quad is a rectangle, so both are linear in Mercator y, while the affine is linear in latitude. Neither overlay splits into strips; only the tiler does. My script (verify/merc.py) reproduces the errors, all at mid-sheet: USGS 4.6 m, 1:50k 15' at -34 10.3 m, 30' at 50N 73.0 m, 1 deg at 50N 294.6 m, 1 deg at -35 173.2 m. Tactical 1:25k/1:50k sheets see only 2-5 pt, but 1:100k and 1:250k JOG sheets are plausible field maps and would be tens to hundreds of metres off the MGRS grid, so high holds.

Both platforms cap the raster at 1 px per point. iOS: boundedPDFRasterSize uses scale = min(1, dimensionScale, memoryScale) (PDFOverlay.swift:83), and PDFRasteriser caps again at :117-121. Android does the same in boundedPdfRenderSize (PdfPageRenderer.kt:55). For the USGS crop the memory budget would allow 1.546x (my calculation) and the dimension cap 2.0x, yet both render at 1.0. Nothing re-renders at screen resolution: the only production caller of PDF rendering on iOS is TileMapContainer.swift:379, via renderedImage, and on Android it is CustomMapOverlays.kt:827, via renderFirstPage. renderFirstPageRegion is called only from androidTest (PdfImportSmokeTest.kt:55). One source pixel is about 8.5 m on the ground for USGS, so zooming past about z14 on a 3x screen just magnifies the blur. This overlay is also where fiduciaries are placed, so taps are imprecise too.

Android never reads CropBox or a MediaBox origin: the only box accesses are GeoPdfParser.kt:68-69 and :362, which use mediaBox width/height. GeoPDF correspondences are in raw user space (the BBox/LPTS math at GeoPdfParser.kt:200-207). PdfRenderer page space, however, comes from pdfium's CPDF_Page::GetDisplayMatrix, which maps m_BBox (the CropBox, else the MediaBox) with its lower-left at the origin, y-flipped, onto an integer rect. PdfGroundLayer pins the bitmap to transform.apply(0..pw, 0..ph) (CustomMapOverlays.kt:858-865), and PdfTiler flips with an integer h (PdfTiler.kt:202-209). Both assume that frame starts at (0,0) with integer size, so a CropBox or MediaBox offset (x0, y0) shifts the sheet by (x0, y0). Cropping in macOS Preview writes exactly this kind of CropBox, so the case is plausible. One correction: the fractional-size part is not a uniform shift. The int/float scale error grows from 0 at the bottom-left to frac(H), about 0.89 pt (about 7.8 m at 1:25k), at the top edge. Manual calibration on Android stays self-consistent, as the auditor says.

I tested this directly rather than relying on the docs. PDFPage.h:117-119 says draw(with:to:) takes page rotation into account and draws relative to the box bounds. Using macOS PDFKit via ctypes (verify/pdfkit_draw.py and pdfkit_draw2.py), I rebuilt PDFRasteriser's CTM (translate by -renderRect.origin, then drawWithBox:.mediaBox). (a) MediaBox [100 100 700 500] with a square at user (155,155): the square lands at assumed-user (55,55), i.e. the box origin is subtracted twice and the content is 100 pt off (outside the 600x400 canvas). (b) MediaBox [0 0 600 400] with /Rotate 90 and a square at (55,55): it lands at context (55,545), outside the 400-pt-tall canvas, so the raster is rotated and clipped. A zero-origin, unrotated control drew correctly at (55,55). The iOS import accepts rotated pages: PDFImportSmokeTests.swift:115-133 checks only that the raster is non-empty. PDFTiler.swift:204-210 uses the same draw call. Android rejects /Rotate in preflight (MapScreenHelpers.kt:433-436). Caveat: this ran on macOS PDFKit, not iOS; the SDK header contract is the same on both.

MapScreen.kt:1950-1953: onDismissRequest is a no-op and confirmButton is empty, so no UI path cancels the Job launched at :2018. The ensureActive() calls in PdfTiler.kt:74/79 are reachable only when the composable scope ends. renderFirstPageStrips (PdfPageRenderer.kt:170-195) constructs a new ParcelFileDescriptor and PdfRenderer per tile and calls openPage(0) per strip; pdfium parses the page content on load. I downgraded to medium: because of D3-02, Android bakes today are small (38 tiles for USGS, about 50 for a typical 1:50k sheet), so the uncancellable window is tens of seconds rather than minutes. It becomes high once maxZoom is fixed.

Android: applyCustomMapTransform coerces zoom to [minZoom, maxZoom] (CustomMapTouch.kt:468), with the source's range passed in at CustomMapScreen.kt:306-307. Programmatic targets are not clamped: frameCameraFor flies to z15/z13 (MapViewModel.kt:223-231), centreOnUser to z15 (:600-605), and the pending target is applied through cameraForTarget with no range check (CustomMapScreen.kt:136-146). A baked sheet with max 13 plus a user inside it gives z15, and any pinch with zoomChange != 1 snaps to z13. iOS: handlePinch clamps to the source range (TileMapView.swift:163-165), while the flyTo zoom is clamped only to 2...19 (TileMapContainer.swift:648). On iOS the snap is small for a USGS-like z16 bake, and several levels for large-scale bakes. TileMath already handles overzoom (tileZoom clamps; TileMath.swift:17-19, TileMath.kt:21-22), so the hard gesture clamp is not needed.

My calculation matches: iw=1727, ih=2031, s=0.999444, so the crop's top edge lands on row 0.822 and the right edge exactly at col 1727.0. PDFRasteriser uses a single uniform scale anchored bottom-left (PDFOverlay.swift:116-137), while placement, pdfPoint and localPoint (:255-261, :288-306) assume the image fills the whole rect. The error grows linearly from 0 at the bottom to 0.82 raster px (about 7 m at 1:24k) at the top. I downgraded to low. The slack is always under one source pixel, so it sits inside the 72-dpi blur of D3-04. It is also purely linear in y, so a manual affine fit absorbs it completely on the live overlay. What remains is a sub-pixel difference between the live overlay and a later bake.

tilingTask and tilingProgress are @State on LayersSheet (LayersSheet.swift:18-19). The Task.detached at :146 outlives the sheet. After the sheet is dismissed and reopened, fresh @State shows the Generate button again (:197/:210-215), so a second concurrent bake can start. The orphaned task still calls mapVM.selectMapSource at :156. The offline_tiles directory is created with FileProtectionType.complete (PDFTiler.swift:44-45); only the final file is relaxed (:105-107). UIBackgroundModes location is set (project.yml:71-72), and there is no background task. The lock-failure chain (new files inheriting .complete, SQLite writes failing about 10 s after lock) is device behaviour and needs a run with the phone locked for 60 s to confirm. The orphan and duplicate-bake problems are confirmed from the code alone.

iOS draw() draws only tiles already in the cache at the current integer tile zoom and kicks off loads for the rest (TileMapView.swift:71-91), over a 0.07-white background (:54). OfflineRasterTileSource loads on a queue and completes via main.async (RasterTileSource.swift:182-190), so at least one frame is blank. UIImage(data:) decodes lazily, so the PNG is decoded at draw time on the main thread. Android draws BACKGROUND and then only cached tiles (TileMapView.kt:200-216), and the tile list is recomputed for the new tz (:108-113). Neither platform falls back to a cached ancestor or child tile. The zoom rounding flips at .5 on both, so the whole viewport flashes dark at each level crossing. That is squarely within the user's 'zoom must not wreck the aesthetic' requirement.

iOS tiles are opaque with a white fill (PDFTiler.swift:56-59, :188-189). They draw the full .mediaBox with no clip to pdfCropRect (:204-210), while the live overlay is cropped to bounds.pdfCropRect (PDFMapSource.swift:67 and :96-97). Coverage is 1.2x the GPTS box (PDFMapSource.swift:57-62), so the collar and legend are baked and cut at arbitrary tile edges. Android fills with eraseColor(WHITE) (PdfPageRenderer.kt:179), and both its overlay (CustomMapOverlays.kt:858-865) and its bake use the full page. The two platforms therefore look different for the same GeoPDF, and the white border band changes at every zoom level.

updateUIView (TileMapContainer.swift:112) calls syncPDF, whose guard synchronously calls pdf.renderedImage() on the main thread (:378-379). renderedImage's own doc comment (PDFMapSource.swift:86-88) says to call it off-main on first use, and cachedRenderedImage (:80-84) has no callers. A grep shows renderedImage() is never called from the import worker, so the first frame after import or restore pays the full PDFKit rasterisation on main. If rendering returns nil, cachedImage stays nil and every updateUIView tries again. Android renders on Dispatchers.IO (CustomMapOverlays.kt:825-833).

A grep for pdfOverlayVisible finds only LayersSheet.swift:174 (the Toggle binding) and LayerVisibility.swift:16/46/64 (storage). syncPDF(source:view:) (TileMapContainer.swift:377) takes no visibility parameter, and updateUIView (:112) passes none. The toggle is persisted and visible but has no effect in the only renderer that ships. Commit 52dc3a7 removed the MKMapView path. Medium or low; I kept medium because it is a broken control in the PDF feature itself.

PDFImageOverlayView never sets layer.minificationFilter, so CALayer's default .linear applies (PDFOverlay.swift:166-181). Android draws with Paint(FILTER_BITMAP_FLAG) (CustomMapOverlays.kt:882) on a bitmap from createBitmap with no setHasMipMap. At z11 the USGS sheet is about 727 device px wide on a 3x phone, drawn from a 1728 px raster (2.4x minification), so bilinear filtering alone will alias dense linework. This is cosmetic, so low.

A grep finds no numberOfTapsRequired or onDoubleTap anywhere, and no zoom +/- buttons. The only 'plus' icons are QuickAddSymbolButton (MapSideToolbar.swift:493) and unrelated dialogs. iOS installs pan, pinch and rotate only (TileMapView.swift:130-136). Android's basemap detectTapGestures handles single taps only (TileMapView.kt:172-176). This is a missing feature rather than a defect, but it matters for one-handed or gloved field use, so low.

I inflated the sample PDF myself (verify/inspect.py). The page /VP 'Map Layers' viewport has BBox [0 2088 1727.95998 56.69373] and LPTS [-0.00708 1 0 -0.00514 1.00708 0 1 1.00514]. The two insets have BBox areas of about 5006 and 3336, both with LPTS [0 1 0 0 1 0 1 1]. On iOS, viewportAffine requires (0.0...1.0).contains (GeoPDFReader.swift:349-350) and returns nil, so largestMalformedDeclaredGeoArea (about 3.51e6) exceeds bestGeo.area and the result is .rejected (:222-226). bounds(from:) then returns nil (:84-85), and the importer uses fallbackBounds at the camera (PDFMapImporter.swift:38-39). On Android, nx/ny outside 0..1 are marked malformed (GeoPdfParser.kt:206-209), the viewport is Rejected (:226-230), and parse returns null (:79). The importer then returns the uncalibrated base (MapScreenHelpers.kt:494). The test at PDFImportSmokeTests.swift:337-339 requires LPTS 1.1 to fail. The documented flagship sample, and probably other USGS US Topo sheets, import without georeferencing on both platforms. This belongs to D1, but it is real.

It should no longer be marked 'needs device confirmation', except that it was run on macOS PDFKit rather than iOS. audit.summary:
How the chain works. iOS: GeoPDFReader either reads an Adobe /VP (it fits AffineFitter to GPTS/LPTS) or an LGIDict (CTM, then Projection.inverse, then DatumShift, then a fit). Manual fiduciaries go MGRS.parse, then Datum, then AffineFitter. Every path ends in one 6-parameter PDF-point to lon/lat-degrees affine (PDFMapSource.placementTransform). PDFRasteriser renders the crop at 1 px per PDF point. PDFImageOverlayView.applyAffinePlacement projects the 4 crop corners through MapCamera.screenPoint (Web Mercator, Double) and places the image as a parallelogram. The grid: TileMapContainer.refreshGrid builds a heading-invariant square with a %.3f fingerprint, then MGRSGridRenderer.build (vendored NGA mgrs-ios, Snyder UTM, WGS84) makes 2-point segments, which MGRSGridOverlayView draws through the same camera. Z-order: mask, PDF, heatmap, grid.

Android: GeoPdfParser feeds the same lat/lon AffineFitter. PdfGroundLayer renders the whole page with PdfRenderer (1 px/pt) and warps it with Matrix.setPolyToPoly (a homography) through the 4 page corners from MapProjection. MgrsGridCanvas calls MgrsGridRenderer.build (mil.nga:mgrs 2.1.3 closed-form UTM) and rebuilds on every camera change. PDF sits below the grid.

What is solid:
- Web Mercator and MapCamera math is identical on both platforms and in Double.
- The PDF and grid read the same camera in the same frame, so there is no lag during animation.
- Skia float32 poly-to-poly error is 0.04 px or less at z21.
- The two NGA UTM implementations are within 1-3 cm of exact and of each other, so the crosshair/header readout matches line positions.
- Norway/Svalbard zones are handled by NGA.
- 1 km chords sag 3 cm or less.
- iOS and Android place the sample within 0.5 m of each other.
- The grid is drawn above the PDF on both.
- NAD83 vs WGS84 is about 1 m (minor).

What breaks the acceptance test:
- The sample is rejected outright (D4-01).
- The lat/lon affine model leaves 6.4 m error on the sample (13.6 pt at z18) and 22-40 m on 1:50k 15' sheets. 3-point fits reach 73-85 m (D4-02/03).
- Every northing label in the northern hemisphere reads one less than the line (D4-04).
- 100 km and 10 km lines are straight chords that split from the printed line: 152-338 m and 1.5-3.4 m (D4-05).
- Labels are mostly drawn off-screen (D4-06).
- Plus datum, tiler, recalibration, zone-edge and level-of-detail issues.

Scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cbrooker-Code-TacticalMaps/d9f42208-9d3f-40e1-9b8b-49fa6c488260/scratchpad/audit/: sample_grid_alignment.py, sheet50k.py, fix_options.py, chord_sagitta.py, nga_utm_compare.py, label_offbyone.py, label_visibility.py, android_recal_tap.py, tiler_rotation.py, skia_poly_precision.py. jcheck/*.java runs the real mgrs-2.1.3 jar.

findings.title: The sample USGS GeoPDF's map viewport is rejected (LPTS slightly outside [0,1]), so the sheet is not georeferenced on either platform
findings.description: In samples/USGS_SF_North.pdf the /VP[0] 'Map Layers' viewport (BBox [0 2088 1727.96 56.69], Measure 424, NAD83 UTM 10N) has LPTS [-0.00708 1 0 -0.00514 1.00708 0 1 1.00514]. USGS writes the GPTS corners slightly outside the viewport unit square. Both parsers were hardened in 1c023de (2026-09-17) to require every LPTS value in [0,1]. That marks the largest (map-body) viewport as malformed. Because it is larger than the valid insets, the whole Adobe selection returns .rejected / Rejected. iOS bounds(from:) then returns nil and the importer uses fallbackBounds, a 10 km square at the camera. Android parse() returns null and the sheet stays uncalibrated at its fallback box. Tests pin the strict behaviour ('LPTS must stay normalised').
findings.failure_scenario: The user imports the documented sample (or any US Topo) and turns on the MGRS grid. iOS shows the quad stretched into a 10x10 km box around wherever the camera was, kilometres from San Francisco, with no relation to the grid. Android shows it uncalibrated. The D4 acceptance test cannot even start.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept LPTS slightly outside the unit square (e.g. -0.05...1.05, or any finite value, since the fit is what matters). Keep failing closed on non-finite values and cardinality mismatches. Once the fit exists, validate it by residual instead (an RMS or UTM-affine residual of a few metres).
findings.proving_test: iOS XCTest plus Android instrumented test: build a one-page PDF with the sample's exact /VP (main BBox/GPTS/LPTS above plus the two small insets with LPTS [0 1 0 0 1 0 1 1]). Assert that GeoPDFReader.bounds / GeoPdfParser.parse is non-nil, selects the main viewport, and maps each LPTS point to its GPTS within 1 m. Today both return nil.

findings.title: PDF to WGS84 is one 6-parameter affine in lat/lon degrees plus a linear screen placement, leaving 6 m (sample) to 22-40 m (1:50k) misalignment against the printed UTM grid
findings.description:
Topo sheets are cast in UTM/TM, so PDF to UTM is exactly affine: the sample fits with a 0.22 m residual at its 4 GPTS. PDF to lat/lon is not affine: a UTM rectangle is a curved trapezoid in lat/lon, and the top edge is tan(phi)*dphi (0.48% at 48N) wider in degrees than the bottom edge. Both apps fit lon=ax+by+c, lat=dx+ey+f. The live overlay is then placed linearly: iOS uses a parallelogram from the TL/TR/BL corners; Android uses a 4-corner homography. The iOS LGIDict path even accepts a fit RMS of up to 50 m. Simulated against the true projection (sample_grid_alignment.py, sheet50k.py):
- Sample (if D4-01 were fixed): printed 1000 m intersections sit up to 6.4 m (mean 2.5 m) from the app grid. That is 3.4 pt at z16, 13.6 pt at z18 and 54 pt at z20.
- 1:50k 15'x15' sheet at 48N: iOS 22 m max (10.6 m mean), Android 25 m. At 60N: iOS 28 m, Android 40 m (Android's whole-page homography extrapolates over the collar). At z16 (1.6 m/pt at 48N) that is 14-25 pt.
- Fitting the affine in Web Mercator metres or using a homography does not help (22-33 m). The error is the UTM-to-Mercator curvature itself.
findings.failure_scenario: The user imports a 15' 1:50k GeoPDF at 48-60N, turns on the grid and zooms to z16 near a sheet corner. App grid lines sit 14-25 pt off the printed 1 km lines, and the offset changes across the sheet, so it cannot be explained as a constant shift.
findings.suggested_fix:
Model the georeference in the projected CRS:
- Take the PROJCS from /GCS WKT or LGIDict, or the MGRS zone of the fiduciaries.
- Fit PDF to easting/northing (exact for UTM-cast sheets).
- Display with a mesh warp whose vertices go through inverse TM and then Web Mercator. Use Canvas.drawBitmapMesh on Android and an N x N set of sub-image layers or a Metal quad mesh on iOS.

fix_options.py: 8x8 gives 0.27 m (48N) and 0.42 m (60N); 16x16 is 0.1 m or less. Keep the lat/lon affine only as a fallback for unknown CRSs, and tighten the 50 m LGIDict acceptance.
findings.proving_test: Shared fixture testdata/geopdf_sf_north.json holds the BBox/LPTS/GPTS/WKT and the list of NAD83 UTM 1000 m intersections. For each intersection, compute the page point via the true PDF-to-UTM affine, run it through each platform's placement (PDFImageOverlayView placement math / PdfGroundLayer corner homography) to screen at z18, and compare with MapCamera.screenPoint(inverseUTM(E,N)). Assert the gap is under 1 pt. Currently the worst is 13.6 pt; for the synthetic 1:50k fixture it is about 50 pt.

findings.title: A 3-fiducial calibration (the documented minimum) misregisters the unconstrained quarter of a 1:50k sheet by up to 73-85 m while reporting RMS 0 m
findings.description:
With 3 points the lat/lon affine is exactly determined. It forces the sheet to be a parallelogram in lat/lon, but a UTM-cast sheet is a trapezoid, so the fourth corner is extrapolated wrongly. The fit passes through all 3 points, so rmsMetres = 0. crossValidated=false is computed but never shown. Android toasts 'Calibration RMS 0m'. The iOS HUD says 'need 3+' and 'Tap Finish to apply'. sheet50k.py places fiduciaries at 1 km intersections about 1.5 km inside three neatline corners:
- 7.5' 1:24k quad: max error 13 m.
- 15' 1:50k sheet: 73 m at 48N near the central meridian (CM), 77 m 2.5 deg off the CM, 85 m at 60N.
- With 4 points the error drops to the D4-02 floor (about 22 m).
Because MGRS input is already UTM, a fit in UTM would be exact with 3 points.
findings.failure_scenario: The user calibrates a plain 1:50k scan by tapping 3 grid intersections (SW, NW, NE) and typing their MGRS. The toast says RMS 0 m. Near the SE corner the printed grid runs 70-85 m from the app grid: 11-13 pt at z14 and 45-55 pt at z16. The GPS dot and waypoints are misplaced by the same amount.
findings.suggested_fix:
Fit fiduciaries in UTM (use the zone of the majority, re-projecting other-zone points into it) and render with the D4-02 mesh warp. Until then:
- Require 4 or more points, or clearly flag 3-point fits as unverified.
- Show the leave-one-out residual rather than the in-sample RMS.
findings.proving_test: Unit test on both platforms using shared fixture testdata/affine_fits.json (new case): a synthetic UTM-cast 15' sheet at 48N, 11.5E, zone 32, with 3 fiduciaries at grid intersections. Predict the lat/lon of a 4th intersection near the SE corner and assert the error is under 2 m. It currently fails at about 77 m. Also assert that a 3-point fit is surfaced as not cross-validated in the UI state.

findings.title: Every northing (horizontal) grid label in the northern hemisphere is one less than its line; 10 km easting labels west of the CM and 100 km letters are also wrong
findings.description:
The label text comes from MGRS.from() of the segment's lat/lon-averaged midpoint, then Int truncation: (northing/1000)%100. A constant-northing UTM line bows poleward of its chord (sagitta 1.5 cm at 38N, 2.2 cm at 48N and 3.4 cm per 1 km chord at 60N). NGA rounds UTM to the centimetre, so the midpoint lands at N-0.02 m and truncates to the previous kilometre.

Verified with the real Android jar (jcheck/GridLabelCheck.java):
- SF view: 195 of 390 labels are wrong, i.e. every horizontal one (the line at N=4183000 is labelled '82').
- A zone 32/33 view: 344 of 656 wrong.
- Southern hemisphere: 0 wrong.

The iOS Snyder replica (label_offbyone.py) gives the same 100%. West of the CM the 10 km vertical labels are also 100% wrong ('9' on the 400000 line). For 100 km lines (jcheck/HundredKm.java), horizontal labels always carry the row letter of the square south of the line. Vertical labels carry the west square's letter west of the CM and the east square's letter east of it. The E=200000 line in zone 10 got 'Y', a letter from zone 9.
findings.failure_scenario: The user compares the app grid with the printed USGS grid. The line printed '4183' carries an app label '82'. The crosshair header just north of that line reads ...83xxx, contradicting the label. Grid references read from the overlay labels are 1 km (or 10 km) south of the truth.
findings.suggested_fix: Label each line with its own grid value, not with MGRS.from of a midpoint. Take the UTM value of the segment's defining point in the line's own zone, rounded to the grid precision (NGA GridLine has the easting/northing it was built from). For 100 km lines, pick one convention (the square to the east/north) and derive the letters from the rounded easting/northing in the line's own zone.
findings.proving_test: Unit test on both platforms: build KILOMETER and TEN_KILOMETER for bounds 37.75..37.875 N, -122.5..-122.375. For each LabelMark, compute the UTM value of its line (from the segment's first endpoint, in its own zone, rounded to precision). Assert text == value digits. Today every horizontal label fails (e.g. N 4183000 gives '82').

findings.title: 100 km and 10 km grid lines are drawn as single straight chords, so at zoom 12 and above they split visibly from the printed line and from the app's own 1 km line
findings.description:
NGA returns one segment per grid cell, so a 100 km cell edge is a single 100 km segment and a 10 km edge a single 10 km segment. Both renderers draw it as one moveTo/lineTo in Web Mercator screen space. UTM lines are curves there. Max chord-to-curve ground offset (chord_sagitta.py):
- 100 km horizontal: 152 m at 38N, 216 m at 48N, 338 m at 60N.
- 100 km vertical: 10-25 m.
- 10 km horizontal: 1.5, 2.2 and 3.4 m.
- 1 km: 3 cm or less.

All three types stay on together (100 km always, 10 km from z8, 1 km from z12), and N=4200000 is also a 1 km line. So the thick 2 pt 100 km line and the 1.3 pt 10 km line visibly split from the correct 1 km line and the printed line. At 38N the 100 km split is 5 pt at z12, 20 pt at z14 and 80 pt at z16. The 10 km split at z18 is 3.2 pt (38N), 5.4 pt (48N) and 11 pt (60N). The 100 km label sits at the chord midpoint, so it floats off its line by the same amount.
findings.failure_scenario: At z14 near San Francisco the user sees the 4200000 northing drawn twice: a thin 1 km line on the printed line and a heavy 100 km line about 20 pt south of it at mid-square. At z18, every 10 km line has a 'ghost' 3-11 pt from the printed line.
findings.suggested_fix:
Densify segments before projecting:
- Subdivide in UTM (e.g. 1 km steps, or adaptively until the screen chord error is under 0.25 pt) and draw a polyline.
- Or, when a finer type is visible, skip coarse-type segments that coincide with finer lines and just restyle those finer lines heavier.
findings.proving_test: Unit test: for every HUNDRED_KILOMETER and TEN_KILOMETER segment in bounds around 37.8N, project the true UTM point at t=0.5 (inverse UTM of the midpoint in metres) with a z14 MapCamera. Assert its distance to the drawn straight segment is under 0.5 pt. Today the 100 km horizontal case gives about 20 pt.

findings.title: Grid labels are almost never on screen: the declutter keeps the copy nearest the top/left of the oversized coverage square, which is off-screen
findings.description:
Geometry is built for a north-up square of half-side hypot(w,h)/2. On a 393x852 pt phone that extends 43 pt above and below and 273 pt left and right of the viewport. One label is emitted per segment. The declutter keeps, per line, the copy with the smallest y (easting labels) or smallest x (northing labels), i.e. the one furthest outside the viewport. label_visibility.py, a replica of both platforms, north-up portrait at SF:
- z12: 2 of 14 easting labels and 0 of 26 northing labels on screen.
- z13: 1 of 7 and 1 of 15.
- z14: 0 of 3 and 0 of 6.
- Northing labels land at x = -265 to -324 pt.
Android uses the same square and rule, with a 55 px bucket.
findings.failure_scenario: The user turns on the grid on a phone in portrait and zooms to z12-15. The lines appear but essentially no easting or northing numbers are visible, so grid references cannot be read off the overlay.
findings.suggested_fix: Choose label positions in screen space. For each line, intersect it with the visible viewport inset by a margin (e.g. 12 pt), place the label at the top edge for easting lines and the left edge for northing lines, and skip lines that do not cross the inset viewport. Compute the label value per line (see D4-04) rather than per segment.
findings.proving_test: Pure-logic test on each platform: camera 393x852 north-up at z13 over 37.80,-122.45. Run build plus the declutter and assert every line crossing the viewport has a kept label whose anchor lies inside [8, w-8] x [8, h-8]. Today it is 0-2 of about 22.

findings.title: Android recalibration records wrong PDF coordinates: taps use an axis-aligned lat/lon box while the page is drawn through the rotated affine
findings.description:
onCalibrationTap turns the tapped lat/lon into a PDF point with pdfPointFor(). That linearly interpolates inside source.coverage, which after calibration is the axis-aligned bbox of the 4 transformed page corners. PdfGroundLayer draws a calibrated or GeoPDF source through the full affine, including rotation and shear. startPdfCalibration seeds the existing fiduciaries, including the 4 auto GeoPDF correspondences, so new taps are mixed with correct points. android_recal_tap.py:
- A 1:50k scan calibrated with 3 deg of skew: a tapped page feature is recorded up to 86 pt away, about 1.5 km on the ground.
- A grid-aligned sheet with 2 deg of convergence: about 1 km.
- The USGS sample: about 0, because its lat/lon affine has no rotation.

iOS converts through the image view's own transform (PDFOverlay.swift:288-299) and is correct.
findings.failure_scenario: The user sees the calibrated map is a few metres off (D4-02/03) and starts Calibrate again to add a 4th/5th point. The new point is stored hundreds of metres from where they tapped. After Finish, the sheet jumps and the grid misalignment grows to hundreds of metres.
findings.suggested_fix: When the source has a calibration transform, convert taps through the inverse of the same mapping PdfGroundLayer uses (transform.inverted().apply(lon, lat)). Use pdfPointFor's bbox interpolation only when uncalibrated, and make it Mercator-consistent with the homography.
findings.proving_test: JVM unit test: build a PdfMapSource calibrated with a 3 deg rotated affine (pageInfo 1400x1950). For page points p on a 10x10 grid, compute ll = transform.apply(p) and assert pdfPointFor(ll) is within 0.5 pt of p. Currently the error is up to 86 pt.

findings.title: The datum is ignored: GeoPDF GPTS are taken as WGS84 whatever /GCS says, and manual calibration offers only WGS84/GDA94/GDA2020
findings.description: The Adobe /VP path reads /GCS WKT only for PRIMEM. GPTS are defined in the GCS datum, but a NAD27, ED50 or Tokyo GEOGCS is used as if it were WGS84. The LGIDict path does apply DatumShift, so the two GeoPDF paths are inconsistent. Typical shifts: NAD27 in CONUS is tens to about 100 m (about 90 m around San Francisco); ED50 in Europe about 100-200 m; Tokyo in Japan about 400-500 m. NAD83, as in the sample, is only about 1 m. For manual calibration, users type the printed grid of a legacy-datum sheet, the MGRS parser assumes WGS84, and the Datum picker cannot say otherwise. The printed legacy grid then coincides perfectly with the WGS84 MGRS overlay, so the acceptance test 'passes', while the whole sheet is displaced from the ground truth by the datum shift.
findings.failure_scenario: The user imports a USGS Historical Topo GeoPDF (GCS NAD27) of San Francisco, or calibrates an ED50 1:50k sheet by its printed grid. The map sits about 90 m (NAD27) or 100-200 m (ED50) from the GPS dot and from waypoints received over sync. With manual calibration nothing looks wrong, because the grids agree.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse the GEOGCS datum or TOWGS84 from /GCS WKT (and EPSG if present), then apply the existing DatumShift/Helmert before fitting. Reject or warn on unknown non-WGS84 datums. Add NAD27, ED50, OSGB36, Tokyo and Pulkovo options with Helmert parameters to the calibration Datum picker, with a visible 'sheet datum' prompt.
findings.proving_test: Fixture GeoPDF: the sample's /VP with /GCS WKT replaced by GEOGCS["GCS_North_American_1927",DATUM["D_North_American_1927",SPHEROID["Clarke_1866",6378206.4,294.9786982]]...] and the same GPTS. Assert the imported placement differs from the WGS84-labelled import by the NAD27-to-WGS84 shift (about 90 m) or that the import is refused. Today they are identical.

findings.title: Tile baking (PDF to MBTiles) drops the affine's rotation/shear, putting printed grid lines 8-13 px off inside each tile with jumps at the seams
findings.description:
Each tile strip maps its lat/lon box through the inverse affine and takes the axis-aligned bbox of the resulting rotated rectangle. That bbox is stretched onto the strip (iOS scaleBy/translate; Android setRectToRect FILL), so any rotation or shear in the calibration is discarded. tiler_rotation.py, max in-tile misplacement:
- USGS sample (lat/lon affine rotation about 0): about 0 px.
- Affine rotated 1.9 deg (a grid-north-up sheet 2.5 deg off the CM at 48N, e.g. NZTopo50- or OS-style grid sheets): 8.5 px.
- Fiduciary-calibrated scan skewed 3 deg: 13.4 px.
Adjacent tiles disagree by up to about twice that at the seams. Generate Tiles swaps the active map to the baked MBTiles, replacing the correctly placed live overlay.
findings.failure_scenario: The user calibrates a slightly skewed scanned map, then taps Generate Offline Tiles to get a sharper, faster map. The printed grid in the baked tiles is now 8-13 px off the app grid and stair-steps at every tile edge.
findings.suggested_fix: Render each tile with the full inverse affine (PDF-to-tile matrix = strip mapping composed with the inverse affine, including b/d terms). Better, render per tile through the projected-CRS mapping from D4-02, i.e. tile pixel, then lat/lon, then UTM, then the PDF affine, using a mesh or per-strip affine in both axes.
findings.proving_test: Pure-function test: extract the strip rect/matrix computation. For a source whose affine is rotated 3 deg, map 9 sample PDF points to lat/lon via the forward affine, then to tile pixels via WebMercatorTiles, and compare with where the tiler's matrix puts those PDF points. Assert the error is under 0.5 px; it is currently about 13 px.

findings.title: Android picks grid detail in physical px instead of dp, so 1 km and 10 km lines appear log2(density) (+1 to +1.8) zoom levels earlier than iOS and the grid is rebuilt every frame
findings.description:
MgrsGridCanvas passes mapWidthPx = hypot(w,h)*density against a lon span measured in dp. The derived zoom is therefore cameraZoom + log2(density). On a density-2.625 phone:
- 1 km lines start at camera z of about 10.1, i.e. 9 dp apart (iOS: z11.5, 23.5 pt).
- 10 km lines start at z of about 6.1, 5.6 dp apart.
- The label bucket is 55 px (21 dp) vs 55 pt on iOS.

The gridBounds remember() keys on centre and zoom, so build() reruns in composition on the main thread on every pan frame. At z10.1 the coverage square is 112 km on a side: 26,316 segments, 29 ms per build on a warm desktop JVM (jcheck/BuildCost.java), several times slower on a phone. That is on top of 26k drawLine calls and label hashing per frame.
findings.failure_scenario: On a Pixel at z10-11.5 with the grid on, the map becomes a dense mesh of 1 km lines with overlapping labels (iOS shows 10 km only), and panning stutters at single-digit FPS.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass hypot(w,h) in dp (or pass camera.zoom directly) to build(), and use a dp-based label bucket. Cache the geometry by a quantised region plus the zoom level, as iOS does, but with a margin that covers the quantisation step (see D4-11). Build off the main thread.
findings.proving_test: Shared-fixture unit test: for camera z10.5 at 37.8,-122.4 with a 411x914 viewport, assert that the Android set of grid types equals the iOS one (100 km and 10 km only). Today Android also includes KILOMETER.

findings.title: iOS keeps stale grid geometry while panning at high zoom (%.3f fingerprint is coarser than the coverage margin), so lines are missing in the newly exposed strip
findings.description: refreshGrid only rebuilds when the fingerprint of region centre and span, formatted '%.3f', changes. A 0.001 deg bucket is about 111 m of latitude (88 m of longitude at 38N). The coverage square only reaches 43 pt above and below a 393x852 viewport. A pan can therefore expose up to (111 m / m-per-pt - 43) pt with no generated cells: about 75 pt at z17, 193 pt at z18 and 430 pt at z19. Lines and segments that lie there (the next row's verticals, the next northing line) are not drawn until the rounded centre changes. Android rebuilds every frame and does not have this problem, so the platforms diverge.
findings.failure_scenario: The user reads a grid reference at z18 and pans north about 60 m toward a 1 km line. The line and the vertical segments above it are missing from the top of the screen, and they pop in only after further panning.
findings.suggested_fix: Quantise the fingerprint in screen units relative to the margin (rebuild when the centre moves more than half the smallest margin), or build with a margin of at least one quantisation step plus one grid cell. Alternatively cache by the set of intersecting grid cells.
findings.proving_test: XCTest on the Coordinator: at z18 over 37.8129,-122.45, call refreshGrid, then move the camera north by 0.0009 deg (same %.3f bucket). Assert that gridView's lines include the northing line that is now inside the viewport. Today it is absent.

findings.title: Zone boundaries are not clipped: neighbour-zone lines and labels intrude up to one grid interval (0.2 km, 6 km or 76 km) past the zone edge
findings.description: NGA's GridZone.lines rounds the draw bounds out to the grid precision (floor/ceil) and only clips horizontal segments. The library's own renderer clips each zone to its pixel range (Grids.drawLines context.clip). The app draws the raw segments with no zone clip. For a view straddling 12E at 48N, zone 33's first vertical line falls west of the boundary: 1 km line 0.22 km in, 10 km line 6.2 km in, 100 km line 76 km in. Each is labelled with zone 33 digits and tilted about 4.5 deg against zone 32's grid. The real Android jar (GridLabelCheck.java) shows 18 (1 km), 12 (10 km) and 7 (100 km) vertical segments drawn entirely outside their own zone. The zone junction itself (GZD line) is never drawn.
findings.failure_scenario: On a 1:50k sheet straddling a 6 deg meridian, the user sees an extra, slightly skewed grid line with a foreign label inside the adjacent zone and may read a grid reference against the wrong zone's line.
findings.suggested_fix: Clip each zone's segments to that zone's longitude/latitude bounds (intersect the segment with the zone polygon, densified per D4-05) before projecting. Draw the GZD boundary with a distinct style.
findings.proving_test: Unit test: build KILOMETER and TEN_KILOMETER for bounds 47.95..48.1 N, 11.9..12.1 E. Assert no zone-33 segment has both endpoints west of 12.0 E and no zone-32 segment has both endpoints east of 12.0 E. Today there are 18 and 12 violations.

findings.title: 100 km lines are always on, so zooming out turns the map into a 6-13 pt mesh with 11k-148k segments rebuilt on the main thread
findings.description:
HUNDRED_KILOMETER is unconditional and there is no GZD-only level. At 38N:
- z6: 100 km lines 52 pt apart.
- z5: 26 pt.
- z4 (iOS start zoom): 13 pt, about 11,130 segments plus a label each (15-33 ms desktop JVM).
- z3: 6.5 pt.
- z2 (minimum): the coverage square spans the world, 148,140 segments, 175-215 ms per build on a desktop JVM (jcheck/LowZoom.java).
iOS rebuilds on every fingerprint change while zooming; Android rebuilds every frame.
findings.failure_scenario: The user zooms out to find another sheet with the grid on. The screen turns grey with 100 km lines and label soup, and the UI freezes for hundreds of milliseconds per zoom step, or per frame on Android.
findings.suggested_fix: Below about z5 draw only GZD boundaries with zone labels; enable 100 km from about z6, as NGA's default config does. Cap segments per frame.
findings.proving_test: Unit test: build the grid for a z4 and a z2 camera, 393x852 at 38N, and assert fewer than about 2,000 segments and a minimum on-screen spacing of at least 30 pt. Today the counts are about 11k and 148k.

findings.title: The live PDF is rasterised at 1 px per PDF point, so above about z15 the printed grid becomes a blurry band and alignment cannot be checked better than about ±4 m
findings.description: boundedPDFRasterSize / boundedPdfRenderSize cap the scale at 1.0 (also 4096 px and 32 MB), so the sample renders at 1728x2031 (iOS crop) or 1728x2088 (Android), i.e. 8.47 m per image pixel. The overlay is then magnified: each image pixel covers 4.5 pt at z16, 18 pt at z18 and 72 pt at z20, bilinearly filtered, on a 3x screen. The printed 1000 m hairline becomes a soft band whose centre is only good to about ±0.5 image px (±4 m), while the vector grid stays crisp. Android's baked tiles also stop at native resolution: maxZoom = floor(log2(pageWidth/lonSpan*360/256)) = z13 for the sample, whereas iOS bakes up to the tile budget (about z16-17).
findings.failure_scenario: The user zooms to z18 to check that the grid sits on the printed line. The printed line is an 18 pt grey smear, so the check is impossible and the map looks broken compared with the sharp grid.
findings.suggested_fix: Render the visible region on demand at screen resolution: re-rasterise the page sub-rect under the viewport after zoom settles, or keep a PDF tile pyramid rendered from vectors at screen scale. Let Android's bake go to the same zoom as iOS.
findings.proving_test: Unit test: for the sample page size, assert that the on-screen size of one raster pixel at z18 is at most 1/screenScale pt (currently 18 pt). For Android, assert that PdfTiler.zoomRange for the sample reaches the same maxZoom as the iOS PDFTiler (currently 13 vs about 17).

findings.title: Android assumes the page's user space starts at (0,0) and uses PdfRenderer's truncated int CropBox size, so cropped or fractional-size GeoPDFs are shifted and stretched
findings.description:
GeoPDF correspondences are in PDF user space. PdfGroundLayer maps bitmap corners to transform(0,ph)...transform(0,0), and PdfTiler flips with h - y, using pageInfo from PdfRenderer. PdfRenderer reports the CropBox size truncated to Int, and renders the CropBox, not the MediaBox origin. Two consequences:
- A CropBox with a non-zero origin (e.g. an Acrobat-cropped collar, [36 36 ...]) shifts the whole sheet by that offset: 36 pt is about 305 m at 1:24k and 635 m at 1:50k.
- A fractional page size (e.g. 2087.5 pt) misplaces the top/right edge by up to 1 pt (8.5 m or 17.6 m), tapering linearly across the sheet.
The sample ([0 0 1728 2088]) is unaffected. iOS stays in user space (crop rect plus .mediaBox), so the platforms diverge.
findings.failure_scenario: The user crops the collar off a GeoPDF in Acrobat and imports it. iOS registers correctly, but Android draws it hundreds of metres off the grid, and the baked tiles are equally wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Read the MediaBox/CropBox with PDFBox and map bitmap corners to the CropBox's user-space corners (llx, ury)... using Double sizes. Apply the same in PdfTiler.pageRectForBand and pdfPointFor.
findings.proving_test: Instrumented test: a PDF with MediaBox [0 0 1728 2088], CropBox [36 36 1692 2052] and the sample /VP. Assert that PdfGroundLayer's corner geometry equals the transform at (36,2052),(1692,2052),(1692,36),(36,36). Today it uses (0,1656)...(0,0), a 36 pt shift.

findings.title: Raster tiles are drawn inflated or pixel-rounded, so baked-PDF tiles sit up to about 0.5-1 px off the vector grid and shimmer during pinch
findings.description: iOS draws each tile in frame.insetBy(dx:-0.5, dy:-0.5): a 0.4% scale about each tile's centre, up to 0.5 pt displacement at tile edges. Android rounds x, y and edge separately to integer px after adding 1 dp, giving up to about 0.5 dp + 0.5 px offset. These rounding steps change frame to frame during a pinch. It matters only for baked PDF MBTiles or online basemaps, not the live PDF overlay, which uses exact float geometry.
